abstract: In electrical engineering practice the problem of converting alternating current to direct current is frequently encountered. In the present stage of the art alternating current has to be employed for the transmission of energy if the distance or the amount of energy exceeds certain comparatively low limits. On the other hand, in many applications of electricity direct current has definite advantages over alternating current; for example, in tramway operation, in hoisting, in driving variable-speed machine tools, etc., and it is usually a combination of transmission and application problems which brings the engineer face to face with the question of conversion.

abstract: We are greatly indebted to Mr. Dutton for the concise way in which he has presented a mass of information on the art of electric welding. I would like to supplement his remarks by dealing briefly with the sister art of oxy-acetylene welding so as to make the subject as complete as possible in the minds of members of the Institute, The two systems do not overlap; they both have distinct fields of usefulness, but the limitations of each system are not generally appreciated. Broadly speaking, electric welding is best suited to butt welding and to repetition work of that type. Oxy-acetylene is more generally applicable to repair-shop work where no two jobs are exactly alike. The old carbide generator for producing acetylene is now obsolete. Its great defects were wastefulness of gas, time lost in cleaning and charging, and waste of oxygen owing to the low pressure of the acetylene. The modern method is by the use of dissolved acetylene. By this process the acetylene is generated at a central supply station; it is then purified and compressed into easily portable cylinders of various sizes. If acetylene is compressed to over 25 lbs. per square inch it is liable to explode with great violence if subjected to heat or concussion. Acetylene cylinders are filled with a porous material consisting of Kapok or granulated charcoal which is saturated in acetone. When the gas is compressed into the cylinders the porous material splits the molecules of acetylene so that, a dangerous condition no longer exists.

abstract: I feel I must congratulate Mr. Andrews on his exceedingly lucid paper on Reaction and Oscillation. There is no doubt that feed back or reaction circuits are an unmitigated nuisance in many localities. To my mind the premature placing of reaction receivers on the market was unwise, and a considerably longer period of experiment should have elapsed before putting these potential instruments of torture in untrained hands. It would not be so serious if the operator merely spoiled his own reception, but the thought that one reaction set improperly handled can spoil the reception of a whole district is intolerable. Great progress is being made in the design of circuits, some of which produce results every bit as satisfactory as the best reaction circuits, without the danger of causing the oscillation and re-radiatiou which is responsible for the weird howls and ungodly shrieks emitted by the badly handled reaction set. One must admit, of course, that there are certain modifications of the reaction principle which cannot re-radiate, and therefore do not annoy other listeners-in: the sets complained of, however, are those employing the crudest form of reaction, that is, reaction which causes oscillations to be directly transferred to the aerial. Reaction is not the only cause of weird noises in the telephones or loud speaker, though it is the direct cause of passing these trials on to your neighbours. Overloading the valves will cause a delightful crescendo whistle to be heard in the telephones. Whistling and howling with the resultant distortion of signals can be caused by placing the coupling transformers too close together, or by running plate and grid wires closely parallel to each other. Neglect in emitting a small fixed condenser across the primary winding of first stage transformer will result in a distinct howl, while a steady drumming sound similar to a machine gun in the distance can be traced to an improper value of the grid leak.

abstract: The subject of electric hoists, as you are aware, is a vast subject, but I do not intend to go into the subject very deeply. The use of electricity in operating hoists for raising coal or ore in mining districts is rapidly increasing. The electric hoist shows its superiority over the other types of hoists by being more economical of power — no power being used when the hoist is idle. It has superior speed control; it is simpler m operation, and has a smaller number of parts to get out of order; it is lighter in weight; more compact, self-contained, and more flexible; it has no reciprocating parts, no smoke, no cylinders to freeze, and does not require a skilled engineer of much experience to operate it. Electric mine hoists have so clearly demonstrated their economy that many large companies within the past few years have found it profitable to scrap all steam mine hoists and replace them with electrically operated outfits.

With the development of long distance wireless communication more attention will probably be paid to the subject, as the successful elimination of “atmospherics” will probably not be achieved until more is known about the origin and causes of variation of the electricity of the atmosphere.

Hardly any electrical engineer, be he a representative of a large firm or in business of bis own, uses electrical appliances throughout his home. In fact, I know quite a number of such representatives who are selling cooking and heating appliances who never use them themselves (except a toaster and an iron).
